Data States: At rest; in transit; in use

slides.title: Rest Transit Use
slides.lead: Data faces a different risk depending on whether it is stored, moving across a network, or being processed; cloud security treats each state on its own terms

points.text: At rest: data stored on disk, volume or bucket, idle
In transit: data moving between systems over a network
In use: data loaded in memory or CPU during processing

slides.notes: "Walk through how the same piece of data passes through all three states during its lifecycle, each needing a different defence. Exam hook: interviewers commonly ask to name all three states with one risk each."

slides.title: Risk And Location

cells: Stolen disk or snapshot read offline

cells.text: EBS volume, S3 bucket, RDS instance

cells: Traffic secretly read or changed on the wire

cells.text: TLS endpoint on a load balancer or API

cells: Memory peeked into on a hacked server

slides.notes: "Walk each row, naming the AWS screen only as a pointer: encryption mechanics come in the following sections. Call out Nitro Enclaves as AWS's answer for data in use, the state learners most often forget."
Cryptography Essentials: Symmetric vs asymmetric encryption; hashing vs encryption

slides.title: Three Core Tools
slides.lead: Protecting data at each state relies on three cryptographic tools, each solving a different problem

points.text: Symmetric encryption: one shared key encrypts and decrypts data
Asymmetric encryption: a public-private key pair replaces key sharing
Hashing: a one-way fingerprint checks integrity, not confidentiality

slides.notes: "Explain that each tool answers a different question: who can read, who proves identity, whether data changed. Mention AWS KMS and ACM as the services built on these primitives. Exam angle: hashing is not encryption because it cannot be reversed."

slides.title: Keys Compared
slides.lead: Symmetric encryption locks and unlocks data with one shared key, such as AES. Asymmetric encryption uses a linked public-private key pair, such as RSA or ECC: the public key encrypts and only the private key decrypts

points.text: AES commonly uses a 128-bit or 256-bit key length
RSA keys are commonly 2048 bits or more, far larger than AES keys
Asymmetric suits key exchange and digital signatures

slides.notes: "AES protects bulk data cheaply while RSA or ECC protect the key itself. AWS KMS uses AES-256; ACM issues RSA or ECC certificates."

slides.label: Analogy: house key and letterbox
slides.title: Keys Compared
slides.notes:
TR analogy: A shared house key used by every family member is symmetric encryption, while a letterbox anyone can post into but only the homeowner's key opens is asymmetric encryption: just as a public key locks data for anyone while only the private key unlocks it.

"AES protects bulk data cheaply while RSA or ECC protect the key itself. AWS KMS uses AES-256; ACM issues RSA or ECC certificates."

slides.title: One-Way Fingerprint
slides.lead: Hashing converts data into a fixed-length digest, such as a 256-bit SHA-256 value, using a one-way function that cannot be reversed. Unlike encryption, standard hashing needs no key and proves data unchanged rather than hiding it

points.text: Same input always yields the same fixed digest
Verifies file integrity; salted, slow hashes also protect stored passwords
One changed bit alters the entire digest

slides.notes: "Hashing is one-way, unlike encryption which always has a reverse. Passwords are hashed and salted, never encrypted, in identity stores. Exam hook: explain why a hash cannot be decrypted."

slides.label: Analogy: fruit into juice
slides.title: One-Way Fingerprint
slides.notes:
TR analogy: Blending fruits into juice is like hashing: the juice proves fruits were used, but nothing turns juice back into whole fruits, just as a digest cannot be reversed into the original data.

"Hashing is one-way, unlike encryption which always has a reverse. Passwords are hashed and salted, never encrypted, in identity stores. Exam hook: explain why a hash cannot be decrypted."

slides.title: Setting Up Transit
slides.lead: These three building blocks combine inside TLS (Transport Layer Security): asymmetric keys set up trust, a symmetric key then encrypts the session, and authenticated encryption checks nothing changed in transit

points.text: Asymmetric cryptography proves the server's identity at connection start
Symmetric cryptography carries the bulk encrypted traffic afterward
TLS uses authenticated encryption to protect message confidentiality and integrity throughout the session

slides.notes: "Tie each tool to its exact job inside TLS: authenticate, encrypt, verify. Keep the three roles distinct so learners do not confuse hashing with encryption. Exam hook: this combination is why TLS is called a hybrid cryptosystem."
Encryption in Transit: TLS handshake; certificates & trust chains; enforcing TLS on endpoints

slides.title: TLS Certs Enforcement
slides.lead: Traffic moving between a browser, a load balancer and a backend database crosses networks nobody fully controls, so it must stay unreadable in flight

points.text: TLS handshake builds a secure channel for one connection
Certificates and trust chains prove the server's identity
Enforcement settings close off any plaintext fallback path

slides.notes: "Frame this as the three pieces the section covers, in order. Stress the order: handshake first, then certificates, then enforcement in the cloud setting."

slides.title: Building The Secure Channel
slides.lead: Before any application data flows, the client and server run a short handshake that agrees how to encrypt, proves the server's identity and creates a shared session key

points.text: Client hello: the client lists the TLS versions and cipher suites it supports
Server hello: the server picks one and sends its certificate
Client checks the certificate chain and that the name matches the server

slides.notes: "Walk the five arrows in order. Stress that the certificate proves who the server is, while the session key is what actually encrypts the traffic; TLS 1.3 completes the handshake in one round trip. Exam hook: ask which key type is used at each stage of the handshake."

slides.title: Building The Secure Channel

points.text: Both sides use key exchange to derive the same symmetric session key
Finished messages confirm the handshake, then traffic is encrypted with the session key

slides.notes: "Walk the five arrows in order. Stress that the certificate proves who the server is, while the session key is what actually encrypts the traffic; TLS 1.3 completes the handshake in one round trip. Exam hook: ask which key type is used at each stage of the handshake."

slides.title: Where Encryption Ends
slides.lead: A cloud load balancer can decrypt traffic itself before forwarding it, or leave the encrypted connection sealed all the way to the backend

points.text: Termination: load balancer decrypts, sends plaintext internally
Passthrough: encrypted packets reach the backend unopened
Re-encryption: load balancer decrypts, then re-encrypts onward
Termination offloads CPU-heavy decryption from backend servers

slides.notes: "Explain why re-encryption is the common production choice for compliance. Ask: why does termination reduce backend CPU load?"

slides.label: Analogy: gate guard and parcel
slides.title: Where Encryption Ends
slides.notes:
TR analogy: A security guard at an office gate opens a sealed parcel, checks it, then seals it in a fresh envelope before sending it inside: just as re-encryption decrypts traffic at the load balancer and encrypts it again before the backend.

"Explain why re-encryption is the common production choice for compliance. Ask: why does termination reduce backend CPU load?"

slides.title: Root To Leaf
slides.lead: A cloud certificate manager automates the trust-chain work: issuing a leaf certificate, linking it to a trusted root, and renewing it before expiry

points.text: Root CA signs an intermediate CA, which signs the leaf cert
Public CA path suits internet-facing endpoints trusted by browsers
Private CA path suits internal services trusted only inside the org
ACM auto-renews certificates it issues; imported certificates must be renewed manually

slides.notes: "Stress that the chain here is managed by a cloud service rather than configured by hand. Mention that a broken intermediate link fails the whole chain."

slides.title: AWS Service Map
slides.lead: Attaching a certificate is only half the job; an endpoint must also be configured to reject any connection that does not use it

points.text: AWS Certificate Manager (ACM): issues certificates that load balancers, CloudFront and API Gateway use
Load balancer HTTPS listener: terminates TLS; plain HTTP is redirected or removed
API Gateway: accepts only HTTPS; a custom domain uses an ACM certificate

slides.notes: "Name ACM as the exact AWS console location, since the topic names a specific tool. Exam hook: ask why aws:SecureTransport in a bucket policy blocks plaintext S3 access."

slides.title: AWS Service Map

points.text: S3 bucket policy: denies requests where `aws:SecureTransport` is false
Minimum TLS version policy: blocks outdated, weaker protocol versions

slides.notes: "Name ACM as the exact AWS console location, since the topic names a specific tool. Exam hook: ask why aws:SecureTransport in a bucket policy blocks plaintext S3 access."

slides.label: Quiz Time
slides.notes: Quiz on Data States, Core Tools and Encryption in Transit. Q1. Name the three data states. Answer: At rest, in transit and in use. Q2. Why is hashing not encryption? Answer: It is one-way and cannot be reversed. Q3. Which key type is used at each stage of the TLS handshake? Answer: Asymmetric keys set up trust, then a symmetric session key encrypts the traffic. Q4. Why does aws:SecureTransport in a bucket policy block plaintext S3 access? Answer: The policy denies requests where aws:SecureTransport is false.
Encryption at Rest: Volume, bucket & database encryption; client-side vs server-side encryption

slides.title: Protecting Stored Data
slides.lead: A stolen disk, a leaked backup or an exposed snapshot exposes whatever sits on it; encryption at rest scrambles that data into ciphertext at the storage layer itself, so a copied file reveals nothing without the key

points.text: Block volumes: the attached disk behind a compute instance
Object buckets: the files written to a storage bucket
Databases: the underlying storage, backups and replicas
Each can be encrypted server-side or client-side

slides.notes: "Open by naming the risk: a lost disk or a leaked backup is plaintext unless it was encrypted before it left the service. State that three storage types get this treatment and a fourth question (where the work happens) cuts across all three."

slides.title: EBS At Rest
slides.lead: Amazon Elastic Block Store (EBS), the block volume attached to an EC2 instance, can be encrypted so every block written to it is stored as ciphertext, decrypted transparently as the instance reads it

points.text: Encryption is set as a flag at volume creation time
Snapshots of an encrypted volume stay encrypted automatically
Data moving between instance and volume is encrypted too

slides.notes: "Explain that encryption happens below the operating system, so the application and OS see plain data while the physical block is unreadable. Flag the common exam trap: an existing unencrypted volume cannot be encrypted in place, only via a snapshot copy."

slides.title: EBS At Rest

points.text: Existing unencrypted volume needs a snapshot copy to encrypt
Enabled from the EBS console's Encrypt checkbox at creation

slides.notes: "Explain that encryption happens below the operating system, so the application and OS see plain data while the physical block is unreadable. Flag the common exam trap: an existing unencrypted volume cannot be encrypted in place, only via a snapshot copy."

slides.title: S3 Default Options
slides.lead: Amazon S3 can encrypt every object written to a bucket by default, so an upload with no encryption header still lands on disk as ciphertext

points.text: SSE-S3: Amazon-managed key, encryption handled entirely by S3
SSE-KMS: uses an AWS KMS key; key usage is logged in CloudTrail
Since 2023 S3 applies SSE-S3 by default; a bucket can be switched to SSE-KMS
Found under the bucket's Properties tab, Default Encryption

slides.notes: "Point out that default encryption removes the need for every uploading application to set its own encryption header. Mention that SSE-KMS trades a little latency for an auditable trail of key usage, which interviewers often probe."

slides.title: RDS At Creation
slides.lead: Managed databases such as Amazon RDS and Aurora encrypt the storage volume underneath the database engine, and that choice has to be made when the instance is first created

points.text: Encrypts storage, automated backups, snapshots and replicas
Read replicas match the source's encryption; cross-Region replicas use a KMS key in that Region

slides.notes: "Stress that the encryption decision is permanent at creation, unlike S3's bucket-level toggle. Give the workaround for an existing unencrypted database: snapshot it, copy the snapshot with encryption enabled, then restore."

slides.title: RDS At Creation

points.text: Cannot be switched on for an existing instance; restore from an encrypted snapshot copy instead
Set via the Create Database screen's encryption option

slides.notes: "Stress that the encryption decision is permanent at creation, unlike S3's bucket-level toggle. Give the workaround for an existing unencrypted database: snapshot it, copy the snapshot with encryption enabled, then restore."

slides.title: Where Work Happens
slides.lead: A second question cuts across volumes, buckets and databases alike: whether the storage service does the encrypting, or the application does it before the data ever leaves
slides.notes: "Stress that server-side is the default across the volume, bucket and database cases, while client-side shifts that same job onto the application. Note the trade-off for interviews: client-side gives stronger control but loses provider-side features like search or indexing on the data."

slides.title: Where Work Happens

cells: Provider or KMS manages the key, depending on the option chosen
Client controls the key; the storage service never sees it

slides.notes: "Stress that server-side is the default across the volume, bucket and database cases, while client-side shifts that same job onto the application. Note the trade-off for interviews: client-side gives stronger control but loses provider-side features like search or indexing on the data."
Key Management: Key Management Service (KMS); provider- vs customer-managed keys; envelope encryption; rotation, HSM & BYOK

slides.title: Protecting The Keys
slides.lead: Encryption only protects data if the keys themselves stay protected, so cloud providers offer a dedicated service to generate, store and control those keys rather than leaving it to each application

points.text: Key Management Service (KMS): central creation, storage and control of keys
Provider-managed vs customer-managed keys: who sets policy and rotation
Envelope encryption: a data key encrypts data, a KMS key wraps it
Rotation, HSM & BYOK: refreshing keys, hardware custody, importing own key material

slides.notes: "Set this as the map for the section before going into KMS itself. Say plainly: data gets locked, but who locks the lock. Interview hook: ask why key management is treated as a separate concern from encryption itself."

slides.title: Managed Key Service
slides.lead: AWS Key Management Service (KMS) is the managed service that creates, stores and controls the cryptographic keys other AWS services use

points.text: Generates keys and controls who may use them through key policies
Integrates directly with S3, EBS, RDS and other storage services
Keeps raw key material inside its boundary, never returned to callers
Key use is recorded in AWS CloudTrail for auditing

slides.notes: "Open with the bank-locker problem before naming KMS. Point to where a key's alias and rotation status appear if a console view is shown. Exam hook: KMS never exports plaintext key material by design."

slides.label: Analogy: bank locker room
slides.title: Managed Key Service
slides.notes:
TR analogy: A bank keeps every locker's key inside its own guarded room, letting a customer use it without ever walking out with the actual key: just as KMS uses a key internally without ever releasing the raw key material to the application.

"Open with the bank-locker problem before naming KMS. Point to where a key's alias and rotation status appear if a console view is shown. Exam hook: KMS never exports plaintext key material by design."

slides.title: Who Controls Keys
slides.lead: AWS encrypts many services automatically using its own keys, but regulated workloads often need direct control over key policy, rotation and audit trail, which is what a customer-managed key provides
slides.notes: "Explain that the choice is about control and auditability, not strength of encryption. Point to the key-policy tab if a console screenshot is on screen. Exam hook: ask which option supports revoking access instantly by disabling the key."

slides.title: Who Controls Keys

cells: Owner can disable or schedule deletion
Set by AWS, cannot be edited
Default EBS encryption, SSE-KMS with aws/s3

slides.notes: "Explain that the choice is about control and auditability, not strength of encryption. Point to the key-policy tab if a console screenshot is on screen. Exam hook: ask which option supports revoking access instantly by disabling the key."

slides.title: Data Key And KMS Key
slides.lead: Encrypting a large file directly with a KMS key is impractical, since the Encrypt API accepts only 4 KB, so envelope encryption uses a fast local key for the data and calls KMS only to protect that smaller key

points.text: KMS generates a 256-bit AES data key and its encrypted copy

KMS key used: ID
`1a2b3c4d-5e6f-7890-abcd-ef1234567890`
Application encrypts a 2 GB file locally with the plaintext data key

slides.notes: "Walk the five steps in order, stressing that the plaintext data key never touches disk. Point to the encrypted-data-key field if a screenshot of an S3 object's metadata is shown. Exam hook: this is why KMS can encrypt unlimited data despite API call limits."

slides.title: Data Key And KMS Key

points.text: Encrypted data key is stored alongside the ciphertext file
To decrypt, KMS unwraps the encrypted data key and the application decrypts the file locally

slides.notes: "Walk the five steps in order, stressing that the plaintext data key never touches disk. Point to the encrypted-data-key field if a screenshot of an S3 object's metadata is shown. Exam hook: this is why KMS can encrypt unlimited data despite API call limits."

slides.title: Refresh And Hardware
slides.lead: A key that never changes becomes a bigger risk the longer it is used, and software-only storage is itself a target, so providers add scheduled rotation and hardware-backed custody as two further safeguards

points.text: Automatic rotation: when enabled, AWS KMS rotates eligible customer-managed key material every year by default
Older key versions are retained to decrypt data encrypted earlier

slides.notes: "Explain rotation as reducing how long a compromised key stays useful, not as changing how data already encrypted is read. Mention CloudHSM only as the dedicated-hardware option, not a deep dive. Exam hook: rotating a key never re-encrypts old ciphertext immediately."

slides.title: Refresh And Hardware

points.text: Hardware Security Module (HSM): tamper-resistant hardware that never exposes raw keys
AWS CloudHSM offers single-tenant, dedicated hardware for stricter compliance needs

slides.notes: "Explain rotation as reducing how long a compromised key stays useful, not as changing how data already encrypted is read. Mention CloudHSM only as the dedicated-hardware option, not a deep dive. Exam hook: rotating a key never re-encrypts old ciphertext immediately."

slides.title: Importing Key Material
slides.lead: Some organisations must use key material their own systems generated, rather than a key AWS creates, for internal compliance; Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) is the process of importing that external key material into KMS

points.text: Key material is generated in an on-premises HSM before import
An import token and wrapping key secure the transfer into KMS

slides.notes: "Clarify BYOK addresses who originates the key, and note AWS does not keep imported material as durable as its own, so the owner must keep a copy. If showing the console, point to the key-material-origin field marked external. Exam hook: BYOK keys can be deleted by the owner to revoke access outside any AWS workflow."

slides.title: Importing Key Material

points.text: Imported keys keep policy control like native keys
But cannot rotate automatically (rotation is on demand or manual)
Owner can delete the imported material, making the key unusable until the same material is re-imported

slides.notes: "Clarify BYOK addresses who originates the key, and note AWS does not keep imported material as durable as its own, so the owner must keep a copy. If showing the console, point to the key-material-origin field marked external. Exam hook: BYOK keys can be deleted by the owner to revoke access outside any AWS workflow."

slides.label: Analogy: own key at a rented locker
slides.title: Importing Key Material
slides.notes:
TR analogy: Bringing your own key to a rented locker instead of using the key provided by the locker facility: just as BYOK lets an organisation use its own generated key material in AWS KMS instead of relying on AWS-generated key material.

"Clarify BYOK addresses who originates the key, and note AWS does not keep imported material as durable as its own, so the owner must keep a copy. If showing the console, point to the key-material-origin field marked external. Exam hook: BYOK keys can be deleted by the owner to revoke access outside any AWS workflow."

Quiz on Encryption & Key Management. Q1. Name the three data states. Answer: At rest, in transit and in use. Q2. Which AWS feature protects data in use? Answer: Nitro Enclaves. Q3. Why is hashing not encryption? Answer: It is one-way and cannot be reversed. Q4. Which key type is used at each stage of the TLS handshake? Answer: Asymmetric keys set up trust, then a symmetric session key encrypts the traffic. Q5. Why does aws:SecureTransport in a bucket policy block plaintext S3 access? Answer: The policy denies requests where aws:SecureTransport is false. Q6. How do you encrypt an existing unencrypted EBS volume? Answer: Through a snapshot copy, never in place. Q7. Which key option supports revoking access instantly by disabling the key? Answer: A customer-managed key. Q8. Why can KMS encrypt unlimited data despite the 4 KB Encrypt limit? Answer: Envelope encryption: a local data key encrypts the data, KMS only wraps the data key.

1. Data States: At rest; in transit; in use
2. Cryptography Essentials: Symmetric vs asymmetric encryption; hashing vs encryption
3. Encryption in Transit: TLS handshake; certificates & trust chains; enforcing TLS on endpoints
4. Encryption at Rest: Volume, bucket & database encryption; client-side vs server-side encryption
5. Key Management: Key Management Service (KMS); provider- vs customer-managed keys; envelope encryption; rotation, HSM & BYOK
